newsitem.title: USA: Mercury Finance troubles touch school districts.
newsitem.headline: Mercury Finance troubles touch school districts.

text.p: School districts in Illinois and Michigan dodged a bullet this week when their short-term investment funds were able to divest themselves of Mercury Finance Co.'s commercial paper without suffering any losses.

AMBAC Indemnity Corp., which recently acquired Cadre Financial Services, Inc., the financial adviser for the funds, said Friday that Cadre had sold all holdings of Mercury Finance commercial paper in the Illinois and Michigan funds at no loss to those funds.

An AMBAC spokesman declined to comment on how much Mercury Finance commercial paper was owned by the funds or if the commercial paper was sold at a loss and if so who absorbed that loss. He said, however, the sales would have no impact on AMBAC's earnings.
Officials at Ronkonkoma, N.Y.-based Cadre, which provides cash management and investment advisory services in 14 states, were not available to comment.

Wayne Sampson, executive director of the Illinois Association of School Boards, said that $1.1 billion of funds the group sponsored through Cadre had $12 million in Mercury Finance commercial paper that was sold this week, days after the consumer finance company's financial troubles became public.
He said it was his understanding that AMBAC bought the paper and had since sold it.

Jerry Keidel, executive director of the Michigan Association of School Administrators, which sponsors school investment funds in that state, said that only a "very small" portion of the $1.3 billion investment portfolio run by Cadre for Michigan schools contained Mercury Finance commercial paper.

Rating agency officials cautioned that local governments should be aware of the credit quality of investments they make. Meanwhile, Illinois Treasurer Judy Baar Topinka called for legislative hearings into tightening her state's local government investment laws.

Mercury Finance last week said it had to restate its last four year's earnings lower by a total of about $90 million after discovering accounting discrepancies. Later in the week, the consumer finance company said it was in default on its short-term lending agreements.
On Monday, the Federal Bureau of Investigation served a search warrant at the company's Lake Forest, Ill. headquarters seeking financial documents.
